title: AI incident response
summary: AI incidents are probabilistic, context-dependent and hard to root-cause. Extend classic incident response with AI harm categories, domain-weighted severity, AI-specific telemetry, staged remediation and a reporting plan, and rehearse it before you need it.
useIf: An AI system or agent can cause harm, leak data or act wrongly, and you must contain it and, for some systems, report it.
avoidIf: You assume your classic security playbook covers it: taxonomy, severity, root cause and telemetry all differ.

explain.md: Microsoft's guidance names four reasons AI incidents are different. **Taxonomy gaps**: harms such as dangerous instructions or targeted content do not fit confidentiality, integrity and availability buckets. **Context-dependent severity**: wrong medical advice and wrong trivia are not the same incident. **Ambiguous root cause**: behaviour emerges from training data, fine-tuning, retrieval inputs and user context. **Telemetry gaps**: standard monitoring does not see output anomalies or classifier confidence shifts, and privacy-by-design defaults narrow the forensic record [[r21]]. A gap in a safety classifier can produce thousands of harmful outputs before a reviewer sees the first.

The prescribed **staged remediation** has three stages. **Stage 1**, the first hour: contain by blocking known-bad inputs, activating content filters and restricting access. **Stage 2**, the first 24 hours: expand mitigations to related variants using automated pattern analysis. **Stage 3**, days to weeks: fix at source with classifier updates, model adjustments and systemic changes. Allow and block lists are tactical, not durable, and each stage needs a **watch period**, because non-deterministic behaviour cannot be verified by one test pass [[r21]]. For **high-risk systems**, providers report serious incidents within 15 days of awareness, within 2 days for a widespread infringement or an Article 3(49)(b) incident, and within 10 days after a death, and an incomplete initial report is allowed. The provider must not alter the system in a way that affects later evaluation of causes before informing the authorities [[r7]]. Deployers who identify a serious incident inform the provider first, then the importer or distributor and authorities, and suspend use if the system presents a risk [[tr1]].

steps.title: Detect
steps.md: Output anomalies, classifier shifts, report spikes, Defender alerts [[r15]].

steps.title: Contain
steps.md: First hour. Disable the identity or tool, block bad inputs, tighten filters, switch to read-only.

steps.title: Expand
steps.md: First 24 hours. Cover related variants, roll back the prompt or model.

steps.title: Fix at source
steps.md: Days to weeks. Classifier, model and design changes. Keep watch periods.

steps.title: Learn
steps.md: Update taxonomy, tests, runbook and records.

whereToUse: Runbooks for assistants and agents with external effects
On-call rotations that include AI quality and safety signals
Regulated deployments with serious-incident reporting duties
Tabletop exercises with security, legal, communications and support
Post-incident reviews that feed evals and guardrails

use: Any production AI system with user-facing or action-taking behaviour
Before launch: define roles, kill switches and reporting paths
After each incident: convert findings into tests and monitors
avoid: Treating a blocklist entry as the fix
Declaring done after one successful test
Altering a high-risk system before the authorities have been informed where Article 73(6) applies
flips: A death or widespread infringement is involved: the 10-day or 2-day clocks apply
The incident is an agent action: suspend its identity first, then investigate
Logs hold no content: rely on ids, versions and decisions, and plan bounded content capture next time

pitfalls.symptom: The system was rebuilt and the root cause cannot be shown
pitfalls.cause: The team altered or deleted the system before preserving evidence or informing authorities
pitfalls.fix: Snapshot logs, versions and configuration first; follow Article 73(6) for high-risk systems [[r7]]

pitfalls.cause: No kill switch or the identity could not be disabled quickly
pitfalls.fix: Build per-tool and per-identity disable switches and test them

pitfalls.symptom: The same harm returns after a fix
pitfalls.cause: A blocklist entry was treated as durable and no watch period followed
pitfalls.fix: Use allow and block lists as triage, fix at source, and watch after each stage [[r21]]

pitfalls.symptom: Responders burn out after a safety incident
pitfalls.cause: Exposure to harmful content with no rotation or support
pitfalls.fix: Plan rotation, breaks and peer support in advance; responders meet harmful content in ways malware analysts do not [[r21]]

scenarios.title: An agent emails the wrong recipients
scenarios.situation: A support agent was steered by a poisoned document and sent account summaries to external addresses. The pattern is spotted after 40 minutes.
constraints: The agent has its own identity
Logs hold ids and decisions but not content
unknowns: Can the sponsor disable the identity immediately?
Which other agents read the same document?
scenarios.question: What do you do in the first hour?

options.name: Disable the agent's identity or send tool, quarantine the document, preserve logs and versions, notify the owners
options.why: It stops the leak, removes the vector and keeps evidence, then expands to related agents.
options.tradeoff: The agent is offline until review.

options.name: Patch the prompt and keep the agent running
options.why: A prompt edit is probabilistic and the poisoned document remains.
options.tradeoff: Right for a stage-3 fix, after containment.

options.name: Wait for the full root cause before acting
options.why: Containment comes before investigation, and the leak continues meanwhile.
options.tradeoff: Waiting is right only when containment would destroy evidence you cannot capture.

flips.if: Several agents read the same corpus
flips.then: In stage 2, quarantine it for all of them.
Start the notification process with legal and the data protection officer.

scenarios.title: Harmful outputs after a model update
scenarios.situation: After a provider model update, user reports of harmful replies triple within a day. No code changed on your side.
constraints: Providers may take days to respond
unknowns: Can you pin or roll back the model version?
scenarios.question: How do you respond?

options.name: Roll back or pin the previous version, tighten filters, then expand to related patterns and watch before closing
options.why: Containment is quick and reversible, and the staged plan covers variants and verification.
options.tradeoff: You may lose features of the new model until fixed.

options.name: Add a blocklist of offending prompts
Wait for the provider to fix it
options.why: Your users are exposed, and the issue may involve your prompt and context.
options.tradeoff: Right only if you cannot influence the model or can switch off the feature.

flips.then: Switch to a fallback model or disable the feature.

flips.if: Reports spike in one language or group

scenarios.takeaway: Roll back to a known-good version, then fix at source.

scenarios.title: A suspected serious incident in a high-risk system
scenarios.situation: A deployer of a high-risk system learns that a malfunction may have contributed to a person's death. The provider is reachable.
constraints: Engineers want to restart and patch immediately
unknowns: When did the provider or deployer become aware?
scenarios.question: What are the first steps?

options.name: Inform the provider immediately, suspend use if a risk exists, preserve the system state, and let the provider report within the 10-day limit
options.why: Deployers inform the provider first and suspend use on risk, and a death sets a 10-day reporting limit. Preserving state avoids altering evidence before authorities are informed.

options.name: Patch and restart first, report later
options.why: Altering the system before informing authorities can affect evaluation of causes.
options.tradeoff: Right only when a safety hazard requires an immediate stop and evidence is captured.

options.name: Wait 15 days for the standard report window
options.why: A death shortens the limit to 10 days, and reports should be immediate once a causal link is suspected.
options.tradeoff: 15 days is the general limit for other serious incidents.

flips.then: Article 73 applies to the deployer as if it were the provider.

scenarios.takeaway: Know the clock before you need it: 15, 2 or 10 days.

quiz.q: Put the staged remediation in order.
items: Immediate containment in the first hour
Expand and strengthen in the first 24 hours
Fix at source over days or weeks
quiz.explain: Microsoft's guidance prescribes three stages with watch periods after each, because one test pass cannot verify non-deterministic behaviour [[r21]].

quiz.q: Match each Article 73 situation to the reporting limit.
quiz.explain: Article 73 sets 15 days after awareness as the general limit, 2 days for a widespread infringement or an Article 3(49)(b) incident, and 10 days for a death. An incomplete initial report is allowed [[r7]].

quiz.q: A blocklist stopped the harmful outputs, then similar ones returned a week later. What was missed?
options: A bigger blocklist is always sufficient
Fixing at source and a watch period after each stage
quiz.explain: Allow and block lists are tactical triage. Stage 3 fixes the classifier, model or design, and watch periods verify the fix [[r21]]. A bigger list leaves variants, and removing logs hurts.

flashcards.front: Why do AI incidents differ from classic security incidents?
flashcards.back: Taxonomy gaps, context-dependent severity, ambiguous root cause and telemetry gaps. Outputs are probabilistic and one gap can cause thousands of harms.

flashcards.front: What are the three remediation stages?
flashcards.back: Contain in the first hour, expand in the first 24 hours, fix at source over days or weeks, with a watch period after each.

flashcards.front: What are the Article 73 reporting limits?
flashcards.back: 15 days after awareness, 2 days for widespread infringement or Article 3(49)(b), 10 days after a death. An incomplete initial report is allowed.
